questions.topic: Idempotent Writes: Same Input, Same Result
questions.question: What does idempotency require from a pipeline job?
options: Repeated runs over the same input leave the target as if the job ran once
Repeated runs over new inputs append one additional copy of every prior row
A failed run never retries after its final acknowledgment is lost
A successful run produces a different timestamp and sample on every replay

questions.topic: Idempotent Writes: Same Input, Same Result
questions.question: Which write pattern is idempotent for a job that owns an entire daily partition?
options: Blindly append the daily rows after every retry and outage recovery
Overwrite the deterministic daily partition with the complete recomputed slice
Assign a fresh random partition to each attempt and retain every attempt
Increment every target amount when the same source event appears again

questions.topic: Idempotent Writes: Same Input, Same Result
questions.question: A task times out after its write succeeds but before the acknowledgment arrives. The retry doubles revenue rows. Which defect is primary?
options: The orchestrator used a stable business key when it retried the task
The transform derived event time from the immutable source record
The sink used a blind append rather than a convergent keyed or overwrite write
The source partition used UTC rather than a changing local timezone

questions.topic: Idempotent Writes: Same Input, Same Result
questions.question: Why can an overwrite job still fail to produce reproducible output?
options: Overwrite operations always duplicate rows before replacing a target partition
Overwrite operations cannot be scoped to one deterministic date partition
Overwrite operations require every source event to have a nullable business key
The transform may use current time, unseeded randomness, or mutable references

questions.topic: Idempotent Writes: Same Input, Same Result
questions.question: A job owns only half of a shared date partition. Why is truncating the whole partition not a safe idempotent design?
options: The repeatable write destroys data owned by the neighboring job outside its scope
The repeatable write preserves both owners and merely increases scan performance
The partition key changes from event time to a stable source business key
The target automatically merges the neighboring rows after every truncate operation

questions.topic: Idempotent Writes: Same Input, Same Result
questions.question: A pipeline calls a nondeterministic LLM during transformation. Which design best preserves replayability?
options: Append every new model response so retries retain all generated alternatives
Cache outputs by stable input hash or version and reuse them during replays
Stamp each response with current time and overwrite yesterday's deterministic slice
Trust short-window duplicate suppression as a permanent correctness guarantee

questions.question: What makes a partition assignment deterministic?
options: It depends on the worker with the most free memory at processing time
It depends on the auto-incrementing batch number assigned to each retry
It is a pure function of stable data carried by the element itself
It is selected from whichever partition currently contains the fewest rows

questions.question: Why does ingestion-date partitioning make historical event replay unsafe?
options: A replay always deletes the source event before reading its event timestamp
A replay assigns every late event to the original event-date partition
A replay converts stable event identifiers into balanced hash buckets
A replay on a later day lands old events in a different target partition

questions.question: A July 20 event arrives on July 25 in an event-time-partitioned pipeline. Where should it be written?
options: Into the July 20 partition, which a lookback replay safely rewrites
Into the July 25 partition, because arrival context overrides event data
Into a random low-volume partition, which prevents deterministic data skew
Into both partitions, because duplication is required for late-arriving records

questions.question: Why is a stable fingerprint modulo 64 preferable to an in-memory process hash for bucketing users?
options: It assigns each user to a new worker-specific bucket on every process start
It reproduces the same bucket for the same user across runs and machines
It guarantees every bucket is exactly equal even when one user dominates traffic
It allows overflow rows to move to whichever bucket currently has spare capacity

questions.question: Two jobs derive dates from the same timestamp using UTC and Asia/Manila. What failure can occur?
options: Both jobs always assign boundary events to identical calendar partitions
Both jobs become nondeterministic only when their bucket counts are powers of two
Boundary events can map to different days despite carrying the same timestamp
Boundary events lose their timestamps because timezones remove immutable event facts

questions.question: A hash bucket is ten times larger because one customer produces most events. Which response preserves determinism?
options: Move overflow events to random buckets according to current worker load
Partition historical rows by the customer's mutable current country instead
Assign a new sequential batch number to each event from that customer
Choose a better stable key or increase bucket count through a controlled redesign

questions.question: What is the defining difference between full and incremental refresh?
options: Full rebuilds from all input; incremental processes only new or changed slices
Full processes only new rows; incremental recreates the complete target each run
Full requires a watermark; incremental cannot store any processing position
Full is always non-idempotent; incremental is automatically exactly-once

questions.question: What role does a high-water mark play in an incremental pipeline?
options: It records the maximum storage price allowed for a full table rebuild
It records the latest processed change position used to select the next delta
It hashes each user into a deterministic bucket based on worker identity
It deletes source rows after they have been copied into a current-time partition

questions.question: A row with updated_at 10:00 becomes visible after a run has advanced its watermark beyond 10:00. What is the standard protection?
options: Advance the watermark further so the delayed transaction is permanently excluded
Switch the target to blind append and accept one duplicate for every delayed row
Reprocess an overlapping lookback window using idempotent writes
Partition by the current run time so the delayed row enters today's output

questions.question: Why can a watermark based only on updated_at fail to propagate hard deletes?
options: A deleted row always receives a future updated_at value before it disappears
A deleted row is automatically converted into a soft-delete event by SQL engines
A deleted row remains in every source delta with a lower updated_at value
A deleted row no longer appears for the filter to select, leaving a target ghost

questions.question: Which workload most strongly favors a full refresh?
options: A small table where rebuilding is cheap and self-healing simplicity matters
A multi-petabyte fact table with a trustworthy five-gigabyte daily change stream
A source with reliable CDC where full scans exceed the annual cost budget
A large target whose only requirement is minimizing bytes scanned each morning

questions.question: Why is a hybrid refresh policy often the professional default for large important tables?
options: Daily full rebuilds accumulate drift while rare incremental runs remove all ghosts
Cheap daily increments handle normal changes while periodic reconciliation bounds drift
Incremental writes remove the need for keys while reconciliation removes source history
Periodic reconciliation makes deterministic partitioning and idempotent writes unnecessary
